questions.q: A public company was incorporated on March 1, 2024. By what date must it obtain the Certificate of Commencement of Business to comply with the Companies Act 2013?
questions.a: The deadline is August 28, 2024 (180 days from March 1). A wrong answer (e.g., "within 1 year" or "no deadline") reveals the student confuses the 180-day rule with other timelines like annual return filing (60 days) or financial year-end. They may not grasp that this is a strict statutory deadline with penal consequences.

questions.q: "Certificate of Incorporation and Certificate of Commencement of Business are the same thing – both allow a company to start business." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: False. Certificate of Incorporation is the "birth certificate" creating legal personality (conclusive evidence of existence). Certificate of Commencement is the "license to operate" obtained after fulfilling capital subscription conditions. A wrong answer shows the student cannot distinguish between legal existence (personality) and legal capacity (authority to transact) – a critical conceptual gap for board exams.

questions.q: A public company issued a prospectus for 10 lakh shares of ₹10 each. It received applications for 8.5 lakh shares. Can it proceed with allotment and apply for Certificate of Commencement of Business? Justify.
questions.a: No. Minimum subscription is 90% of issue size = 9 lakh shares (SEBI guideline). 8.5 lakh shares = 85% < 90%. Allotment cannot be made; application money must be refunded. Without minimum subscription, the declaration for Commencement Certificate cannot be filed. A wrong answer (e.g., "yes, if directors pay for qualification shares") reveals misunderstanding that minimum subscription is a non-negotiable statutory threshold, not waivable by director contributions.

questions.q: Compare the legal position of a contract signed by a company: (a) after Certificate of Incorporation but before Certificate of Commencement, (b) after Certificate of Commencement. What is the key difference?
questions.a: (a) Contracts after Incorporation but before Commencement are **provisional contracts** – binding only after Commencement Certificate is obtained. (b) Contracts after Commencement are fully enforceable immediately. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are void" or "both are valid") shows confusion between preliminary contracts (pre-incorporation, not binding) and provisional contracts (post-incorporation, conditional). This distinction is a frequent board exam trap.

questions.q: A private company argues: "We don't invite public subscription, so we don't need minimum subscription. Therefore, we can get Certificate of Commencement immediately after incorporation without any declaration." Critique this argument using Companies Act 2013 provisions.
questions.a: Invalid argument. Per NCERT, **both public and private companies** must obtain Commencement Certificate within 180 days. Private companies must still file a declaration that directors have paid for qualification shares and the company has received subscription money (though no 90% SEBI rule applies). A wrong answer reveals the student missed the "both public and private" phrasing in the textbook summary and assumes private companies are exempt – a common error from misreading the scope.

questions.q: Design a compliance checklist for a newly incorporated public company's Company Secretary to ensure timely obtainment of Certificate of Commencement of Business. Include all statutory conditions and deadlines.
questions.a: A good checklist includes: (1) Verify all directors paid for qualification shares (by Day 30), (2) Ensure minimum 90% subscription achieved (by Day 60), (3) Confirm all application money received in separate bank account (by Day 60), (4) File declaration in Form INC-20A with ROC (by Day 150 to allow buffer), (5) Attach bank statement proving receipt of subscription money, (6) If no prospectus issued, file statement in lieu of prospectus 3 days before allotment. A poor checklist misses the 180-day deadline, omits the separate bank account requirement, or confuses qualification shares with minimum subscription.
